Neotropic cormorant eggs incubated under controlled laboratory conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after 26 days [ab = 26 days], a developmental period that aligns closely with incubation durations reported for other members of the Phalacrocoracidae. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of 30 grams [Wwb = 30 grams], a relatively modest neonatal mass that is consistent with the altricial developmental mode observed in this species, wherein parents provide intensive brooding and repeated feeding visits. This initial body size belies a rapid growth trajectory, as nestlings are provisioned with regurgitated fish meals multiple times daily throughout the early nestling period. The 26-day incubation interval represents a considerable energetic investment for the attending adults, who alternate shifts with considerable coordination to maintain stable thermal conditions within the nest, thereby ensuring optimal embryonic development before the vulnerable chick phase begins in earnest. Several comparative studies have noted that cormorants generally exhibit moderate incubation periods relative to other waterbirds of similar adult body mass.

Field observations of breeding colonies in southern Brazil indicate that females typically initiate egg-laying in early spring, although the timing of first reproduction exhibits some latitudinal variation across the species extensive Neotropical range. At a body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], which represents the typical active metabolic core temperature maintained by adults during foraging and nesting bouts, the time since birth at first brood occurs at 365 days [tR = 365 days]. This relatively rapid onset of breeding, achieved within the first year of life, likely reflects the selective pressures of a highly seasonal environment where ephemeral prey pulses, such as annual fish spawning aggregations, must be exploited promptly upon reaching somatic maturity. The ability to commence reproduction in the first year is not universal among cormorants; larger congeners often delay first breeding for two or more years. This interspecific variation suggests that ecological context, particularly the predictability and abundance of local forage fish stocks, plays a pivotal role in governing the timing of first reproductive attempts in Phalacrocorax brasilianus.

Under the same thermal conditions of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] that characterize active metabolism in this species, fledging, defined as the point at which young achieve sustained flight and depart the nest, occurs at 31 days since birth [tx = 31 days since birth]. This relatively early fledging age, compared to some larger waterfowl, allows young to vacate the often crowded and parasite-laden colony site before the end of the breeding season. The energetic cost of feather development during the final week of the nestling period is substantial, and chicks must attain sufficient wing loading to support powered flight over open water. Furthermore, puberty, marking the maturation of the gonadal axis, is reached at 93 days since birth [tp = 93 days since birth] under these same thermal regimes at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The gap between fledging and sexual maturity underscores a critical post-independence phase during which juveniles refine foraging skills, accumulate body condition, and navigate the social hierarchies that will ultimately determine their access to future breeding territories within dense nesting aggregations.

Long-term mark-recapture studies have documented that the maximum recorded longevity for Neotropic cormorants in natural populations, measured at a body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], is 12.6 years [am = 12.6 years]. This lifespan is comparable to that observed in several other medium-sized cormorants and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by moderate annual survival rates among adults and a relatively high potential for reproductive output over the course of a decade or more. The ultimate wet weight attained by full-grown adults reaches 1550 grams [Wwi = 1550 grams], placing Phalacrocorax brasilianus within the mid-range of body sizes for the genus. Larger individuals, particularly breeding males, may achieve even greater masses during the pre-breeding period when fat reserves are accumulated for the energetically demanding incubation and brooding shifts. Body size in this species is also subject to considerable geographic variation, with individuals from higher latitudes tending toward slightly larger asymptotic masses, a pattern consistent with Bergmann's rule across the expansive Neotropical distribution of this cormorant.

Reproductive output in Neotropic cormorants is best described through two complementary metrics that together capture the species annual breeding effort. Females typically lay a clutch of 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt], and in most populations they produce approximately 1 clutch each year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch each year]. This annual reproductive strategy means that the maximum reproductive rate, computed from the product of clutch size and annual frequency, equates to approximately 3.3 eggs per year under optimal conditions at a body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. Brood reduction is not uncommon, as hatching asynchrony can lead to competitive disparities among siblings, with the youngest chick often perishing during periods of food scarcity. Nonetheless, the combination of moderate clutch size and strict single-broodedness allows parents to allocate substantial parental care toward each nestling, enhancing fledgling quality and subsequent first-year survival in this long-lived aquatic predator.
